caption:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman met about 50 senior Samsung executives in Yongin, South Korea, on Saturday.
The talks come as AI data centers fight over scarce memory chips, and Samsung is OpenAI's memory partner for Stargate.
Samsung announced no new supply deal. Altman did hand over a Codex Micro Keyboard as a gift.

Who wins the memory race: AI data centers or everyone else?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Tom's Hardware, NewsBytes · Photo: OpenAI, Samsung

paragraphs.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman met about 50 senior Samsung executives in Yongin, south of Seoul, on Saturday, October 31, 2026. The group included leaders of Samsung's electronics, financial and biotechnology affiliates, according to NewsBytes and Tom's Hardware, which cited a Bloomberg report and said Samsung Korea confirmed the meeting.

Samsung hosted the session. The company said the conversation covered the direction of AI technology development, its potential applications and new business opportunities. NewsBytes reported that the discussion also looked at how AI could change industries and corporate decision making over the next decade.

Samsung did not announce a new memory supply agreement at the meeting, Tom's Hardware reported, and instead emphasized AI transformation and future business. Altman gave the head of Samsung's AI Center a Codex Micro Keyboard, a device made for use with OpenAI's Codex coding agent.

The two companies already have a framework in place. On October 1, 2025, OpenAI signed a letter of intent with Samsung Electronics, Samsung SDS, Samsung C&T and Samsung Heavy Industries covering global AI data center infrastructure, according to Samsung. Under it, Samsung Electronics agreed to act as a strategic memory partner for OpenAI's Stargate initiative, supplying DRAM and other semiconductor products.

In that announcement, Samsung said OpenAI's projected memory demand could reach as much as 900,000 DRAM wafers per month. Samsung C&T and Samsung Heavy Industries also agreed to work with OpenAI on floating data centers, which Samsung said could ease land shortages and cut cooling costs. NewsBytes reported that the latest meeting strengthened the memory supply arrangement and that work on AI data centers, including floating offshore sites, continues.

The visit comes during a shortage of memory chips. Tom's Hardware cited TrendForce estimates that DRAM supply will fall 1% to 2% short of demand this year, with the gap expected to widen in 2027, and noted that Micron has warned the shortage could last into 2028 because new factory capacity takes years to build.

Samsung sits at the center of that market. Citing Counterpoint Research, Tom's Hardware reported that Samsung and SK hynix together held about 63% of global DRAM revenue and about 83% of high bandwidth memory revenue in the second quarter of 2026. High bandwidth memory is the stacked memory used alongside AI accelerators.

Other chip buyers have made the same trip. AMD CEO Lisa Su visited Samsung earlier in October to discuss more high bandwidth memory supply, Tom's Hardware reported. NewsBytes said Su and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang have each visited South Korea twice since last year, and that memory chips account for nearly a third of data center spending.

The meeting also followed recent comments from Altman that drew criticism online. In a podcast interview, he described it as "quite terrible" that so much DRAM sits underused in personal computers and suggested data centers could use memory more efficiently, Tom's Hardware reported.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the meeting shows how much leverage memory makers now hold over AI companies. A visit to roughly 50 executives across Samsung's businesses suggests OpenAI wants a relationship that reaches beyond chip orders, from data center construction to enterprise use of its tools, while supply stays tight for every buyer.
Watch whether Samsung or OpenAI announces firm memory volumes for Stargate in the coming months, since the 2025 agreement was a letter of intent rather than a binding supply contract.
